source.title: Exploring how OthelloGPT computes its world model

record.tranche_reason: The post reports experiments on OthelloGPT neuron rules and their ablation, but does not test whether neurons respond to several unrelated inputs or any of the listed versions of that claim.
record.gate_note: The neuron-rule classification and ablation results are relevant to the broader question of individual-neuron interpretability, but do not measure polysemanticity as defined by the claim versions. The attention-circuit findings and legal-move results do not bear on those versions.
record.test_reason: The post classifies OthelloGPT MLP neurons by fit to hand-defined flipping rules and ablates all others. It never measures whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs, how common that is, or what causes it. So no version of the polysemanticity claim is tested. The weak ablation result bears on whether individual neurons implement interpretable rules, a related but different question.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The author says the failed flipping-circuit ablation gives mild evidence against individual OthelloGPT neurons performing interpretable rules. The author caveats that only a narrow rule set was tested and a code bug is possible. The previous color circuit is called only a rough approximation of what the attention layers do.
record.recipe_differences: The post uses rule-based neuron classification and mean ablation in OthelloGPT; it does not reproduce the methods of the listed original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: The flipping-circuit result varies by layer; the post notes an exception in later layers, where many neurons remain unabated. Center and rim tiles and two ablation variants are plotted separately, but their numerical differences are not stated.

fits_no_version.finding: Neurons classified by a mean-activation-difference rule as following specific flipping rules, kept while all other neurons were mean-ablated, did not reproduce probe flip changes better than ablating all neurons, except in later layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neurons that appear monosemantic for interpretable rules under weight projection and activation thresholds may not be sufficient to implement those rules causally.

fits_no_version.finding: The number of neurons matching each flipping rule varied widely; most rules had 0 or a handful, some had many, especially in later layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Rule-neuron correspondence counts in OthelloGPT vary across rules and layers.

record.problems: The author says only one example was tested thoroughly and notes that a bug in the code is possible. The main ablation comparison is presented in figures without numerical values in the text; the late-layer exception is attributed to many neurons not being ablated.
record.rows_left_out: Left out the attention-head and previous-color-circuit findings, which concern attention computation rather than neuron polysemanticity or rule-neuron ablation. Also left out the legal-move ablation result because it tests move prediction, not neuron meaning.

untested.parts: All: vision classifiers are not studied.
All: no measure of neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts, or of its share by layer.
All: architecture, activation function and regularization are not varied.
All: the 0.17 activation-difference threshold is a classification choice, but its effect on polysemanticity judgments is not studied.

record.verdict_notes: The author calls the flipping neurons 'mono-semantic' based on weight projections, but never tests whether they respond to other, unrelated inputs. No polysemanticity rate is reported. The claim's original sources are not involved. The record's T6 tranche and 'discusses' relation are kept.

versions.untested_parts: Unrelated token or context responses and their prevalence across language-model MLP neurons or layers.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by superposition or capacity pressure.
Polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure, including effects of initialization, regularization, or training noise.
Effects of activation function, architecture, or regularization on the share of polysemantic neurons and performance.
Whether neurons previously judged polysemantic detect one shared feature or related offshoots of one job.
Whether polysemanticity judgments change with activation range or explanation-scoring methods.

rows.operation_detail: Classified neurons as matching flipping rules when their mean activation difference exceeded 0.17, computed over 10,000 games.

rows.measure: Number of neurons corresponding to each flipping rule
rows.value: Figure only; the text says most rules had zero or a handful of corresponding neurons, while some had many, especially in later layers.
rows.note: This measures correspondence to a defined set of rules, not whether a neuron responds to unrelated inputs.

The text says it does not exceed the baseline except in later layers, where many neurons are kept. Relative to the post's own hypothesis this is closer to absent.
